messages.author: d7d0f289cbad9e73
messages.subject: Smoothing functions
parts:
Hi,

I am a new DSM module user. I’m constructing smoothing functions following the Dolphins sample project (which comes with Distance) and Miller et al 2013, appendix A. When modeling latitude and longitude as covariates, Miller applies a vibariate smoothing function, s(x, y), whereas in the dolphins project these covariates are set in two separate functions.

Is there any reason to decide between one choice or the other?

Thanks.

Alejandro

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Smoothing functions
parts:
Hi Alejandro & other listfolk,

I think this difference is purely down to historical reasons (there is a
considerable gap in time between the project being created and the
example written in the appendix). Sorry for the confusion.

Both separate smoothing of spatial covariates and bivariate smoothing
are valid approaches. Generally you might like to include two separate
covariates and see if one or both prove to be useful in the model (by
looking at the EDFs of these components and their p-values, inspecting
plots etc). One can also fit another model with the bivariate spatial
smoother instead of the two separate spatial smooths and compare model
fit based on AIC/REML/GCV and model checking plots (gam.check etc, as
detailed in the paper).

I have seen some data set where for example longitude does not play a
major role but latitude does and vice versa. As we say in the MEE paper,
these covariates are often proxies for covariates that we don't have
measurements (such as distance to a geographical feature like a mountain
range or sea shore), to they may not be particularly informative
biologically even if they appear to explain a lot.


Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

messages.author: 5ea4fdd6f7e361d3
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Smoothing functions
parts:
Hi Alejandro & David,
Thanks for that explanation.  David, wouldn't you say that survey design/coverage probability is another factor to consider?  Several years ago, while analyzing data from a non-systematic (platform of opportunity) survey (http://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol11/iss1/art1/) Sharon Hedley gave me a great example to illustrate this choice.  Imagine a really bad survey, with one N-S transect and one E-W transect.  If you modelled that as 2 separate univariate smooths, your rugplot would look like you had good coverage across latitude and longitude.  In fact, it's terrible spatial coverage.  A bivariate smooth would better reflect that gappy coverage -- in other words, it would let your model know that your smoothed interpolation was really extrapolation.  Is that a fair summary?  In British Columbia, we did a systematic line transect survey with even coverage probability, and the predicted density surfaces for frequently seen species were pretty similar between 2 univariate or 1 bivariate smooth (application described here: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2013.00479.x/abstract).  I'm going back about a decade, but I was also taught that one might rely on different diagnostics depending on whether you're primarily interested in distribution and abundance (e.g., semivariograms to check for unmodelled spatial autocorrelation).  The methods have evolved a lot since then.  I need to reread your MEE paper, David.

I'd also be interested in whether you'd give different advice depending on whether there is collinearity between an ecologically relevant variable and a spatial one.  For example, in our Antarctic minke whale survey (http://www.nature.com/srep/2014/140313/srep04170/full/srep04170.html), Natalie Kelly found that it was best not to include latitude as a covariate, because it was highly correlated with ice concentration.  We did use longitude.  

Maybe you could tell us a bit more about your study & data, Alejandro?

All the best,
Rob

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Smoothing functions
parts:
Rob, you raise some important points and my initial reply didn't
consider these more specific issues.

The issue of collinearity (or more general correlation -- perhaps not
linear) between covariates is important and should be considered when
thinking about which covariates to include in the model as well as
during the model selection/model criticism stage. In this case it seems
that exploratory plotting is a useful tool. I also agree this can be
dependent on the survey data you have -- again exploratory analyses can
inform the modelling process and help avoid unrealistic models.


best,
--dave
